newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB'S GEHRIG - too-weak Swiss franc would be inflationary.
newsitem.headline: SNB'S GEHRIG - too-weak Swiss franc would be inflationary.

text.p: Swiss National Bank (SNB) directorate member Bruno Gehrig on Friday dismissed any ideas that Switzerland would allow a significant devaluation of the Swiss franc, which would threaten price stability.
The call for a weaker Swiss franc to bolster exports has intensified after recent data showed the economy still soft.
"I think the long-term effect of such a move would be disasterous ... because of inflation," he said.

Gehrig also said there were limits on the amount of expansion that the SNB could allow, but did not specify those limits except to say the SNB continued to observe its medium-term monetary expansion goals.
He said the SNB meanwhile would continue providing the economy with enough liquidity, and at money market rates, to fuel an improvement.
"We will basically continue on the same path as we have been," Gehrig said.

Speaking to reporters here during a meeting of the Swiss Bankers Association, he said that a sustained drop in the franc over a longer time period would pose a "disasterous risk" to Swiss price stability.
"I do not think it would be appropriate to say we should push the franc significantly down and then we are out of the problem," Gehrig said.
Gehrig did not specify how much the franc would have to weaken before it posed a significant danger to price stability.
The Swiss franc was weakened slightly versus other currencies in recent weeks after peaking at four-month highs against the dollar in late July.
It traded at 1.2425 francs to the dollar this morning. The dollar had slipped as low as 1.1840 francs at the end of July.

The SNB has said in the past that is worried about an overvaluation of the franc, which hurts Swiss exports. It has in the last two months worked to keep money market rates low, hoping to discourage speculative demand for the franc.
Inflation in Switzerland is currently near zero, and some SNB officials view prospects of deflation, rather than inflation as the greatest risk.

Earlier this week, the Swiss government reported that the country's gross domestic product in the second quarter fell by 0.9 percent, its sixth straight quarterly decline measured against the previous quarter.
Gehrig said the SNB would continue to provide money market liquidity for the time being, saying such moves were aimed at helping the economy.
He was optimistic that the Swiss economy would rebound in the coming three to four quarters.
Asked about the prospects for a recovery in the Swiss economy, Gehrig said: "I am reasonably optimistic for the next three to four quarters."
